title: Power, Prudence, and Restraint in Fénelon’s Telemachus
gist: Iskander Rehman revisits Fénelon's The Adventures of Telemachus as a mirror for princes with three lessons—power isolates rulers from truth, prudence rests on self-mastery, and moderation and trust beat coercion in foreign policy—applying them to Putin's information bubble, Trump's February 2026 decision for war with Iran, China's South China Sea build-out, and the self-consuming nature of tariff and trade coercion.

insights.claim: Hyper-concentration of power tends to narrow advisory circles, distort information flows and produce brittle decision-making, so personalist rulers grow more powerful yet less able to perceive reality.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Personalist regimes carry elevated risk of policy miscalculation and sudden reversals.
insights.quote: even as personalist rulers become more powerful, they also become less capable of accurately perceiving the world around them

insights.claim: Four years into the war, Putin's wartime information environment has narrowed further, with optimistic briefings, curated information and fear of elite dissent detaching him from battlefield reality.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Russian decision-making may be systematically over-optimistic, prolonging the war.

insights.claim: Fénelon's lesson is that good rule requires actively forcing open channels for disagreeable information, not merely resisting flattery, and that weak, impressionable rulers fail as often as wicked ones.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Leadership quality assessment should weight information-channel openness.
insights.locator: In contrast, one of the book’s more virtuous

insights.claim: Fénelon's six pre-war questions function like pilot and surgical checklists for the use of force: interrogate legal grounds, discount interested advocates, seek the strongest counter-case, hear dissent safely, let counselors speak before the sovereign reveals his preference, and separate national necessity from personal glory.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Provides a lens to judge the quality of government war decisions and their risk.
insights.locator: Read in this light, Fénelon’s questions

insights.claim: The national security adviser's honest-broker role, exemplified by Brent Scowcroft, and JFK's ExComm in the Cuban Missile Crisis show how process can slow the rush to action and surface alternatives.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Weak NSC process is a signal of higher escalation risk.
insights.locator: No checklist, of course, can manufacture prudence.

insights.claim: The February 2026 decision to go to full-blown war with Iran illustrates a failure of deliberative process: senior officials reportedly doubted imminent regime change and warned of munitions depletion and Hormuz navigation risks, yet Trump absorbed mainly reinforcing advice.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Suggests the Iran war rested on optimistic assumptions, with munitions and shipping risks under-weighted.
insights.quote: the February 2026 decision to go to full-blown war with Iran provides a useful — and stark — reminder

insights.claim: Regional actors' forceful advocacy and optimism about military action reportedly had more influence on Trump's Iran decision than cautionary assessments from US intelligence and the national security apparatus.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Foreign 'interested counsel' may continue to shape US escalation choices in the Middle East.

insights.claim: States often mistake accumulating power for gaining security; defensive fortification read as offensive by neighbors creates a security dilemma that exhausts the builder's strength.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Arms build-ups can be self-defeating, fueling regional counter-balancing and defense spending.
insights.quote: Kingdoms, Fénelon argues, all too often mistake the accumulation of power for the acquisition of security
insights.locator: What self-command is to the prince

insights.claim: China frames its South China Sea artificial-island bases as defensive, but neighbors see runways, missile systems and surveillance infrastructure as platforms for sustained power projection.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Sustains regional balancing and Asian defense demand.
insights.locator: The contemporary relevance is not difficult

insights.claim: Contrary to Machiavelli, Fénelon argues that being trusted beats being feared because frightened neighbors have armies, allies and long memories and will coalesce against an aggressive hegemon, as the fictional Adrastus discovers.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Coercive hegemony risks provoking counter-coalitions that erode the coercer's position.
insights.quote: frightened neighboring states possess armies, allies, self-pride, and — perhaps most importantly — long institutional memories

insights.claim: Fénelon saw military overextension, oppressive taxation, luxury and foreign ambition as one interconnected pathology of a state burning its domestic foundations to fund fruitless ventures abroad.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Links fiscal strain to foreign overreach, a macro lens on war-driven deficits.
insights.locator: This argument runs through Fénelon’s later

insights.claim: Economic coercion can punish targets in the short term while teaching them to substitute away from the coercer, making coercive leverage ultimately self-consuming.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Tariff and sanctions regimes accelerate trade diversion that permanently erodes the coercer's market share.
insights.quote: coercive leverage can ultimately be self-consuming

insights.claim: After China restricted Australian exports post-2020, wine was badly hit but coal, barley and other commodities found alternative buyers, with Australia's Productivity Commission finding substantial trade diversion.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Commodity exporters can reroute under coercion; differentiated goods are more vulnerable.

insights.claim: The Trump administration's sweeping tariffs have encouraged Canada and the European Union to accelerate trade diversification and reduce exposure to the American market.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Persistent tariff policy may structurally reduce US export market share and reroute trade flows.

insights.claim: Once suppliers and logistics networks bear the cost of building alternatives, old trading relationships may be hard to reconstruct, so reputations for reliability are strategic assets.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Trade diversion caused by tariffs may persist even if tariffs are rolled back.
insights.quote: old trading relationships may prove difficult to reconstruct

insights.claim: Fénelon's depiction of tariff-obsessed Pygmalion driving trade away from Tyre captures the logic that making commerce less convenient creates a habit of trading without you.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Historical framing for the long-run costs of protectionism.
insights.quote: a habit will soon be contracted of trading without you
insights.locator: Time and again, The Adventures of Telemachus

insights.claim: The Adventures of Telemachus became the most widely read book in 18th-century France after the Bible, and censorship of its first printing only stimulated demand.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Historical anecdote that suppression fuels demand for dissenting content.
insights.quote: The Adventures of Telemachus had become the most widely read book in 18th-century France after the Bible.

insights.claim: The book shaped statecraft vocabulary widely: Jefferson topped his reading list with it, John Adams drew on it for his Defense of the Constitutions, and Catherine the Great annotated a copy for her grandson Alexander.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Context on enduring ideas about restraint in statecraft.

insights.claim: In an age of personalist rule, geopolitical volatility and fraying coalitions, the author argues Fénelon's lessons in truth-telling, self-command and strategic humility are urgent.
insights.speaker: Iskander Rehman
insights.so_what: Frames current geopolitics as a regime of elevated leader-driven risk.
insights.locator: Perhaps one of Fénelon’s most important
